name: Meats
description: Chicken, turkey and lean beef are excellent sources of animal protein and easy for a cat to digest.
whyGood: Rich in high-quality protein, essential for a cat's muscles and energy.
howToServe: Cooked and plain, with no bones or skin. In small portions, alongside a balanced diet.
avoid: Raw meat, bones, very fatty skin, and seasonings (salt, garlic, onion, spices).
tip: Vary the protein sources — chicken, turkey, fish — for a balanced diet.

name: Fish
description: Salmon and mackerel provide omega-3s that benefit the skin and coat.
whyGood: Sources of omega-3 and lean protein, good for the skin and the coat.
howToServe: Cooked, boneless, in small amounts and only occasionally.
avoid: Raw fish (risk of parasites), fish in excess (it can unbalance vitamin B1 intake), and tuna in large quantities.
tip: Once or twice a week at most, and never as the only source of protein.

name: Eggs
description: Cooked egg is a good source of complete protein and is well tolerated by most cats.
whyGood: Complete protein, easy to digest once cooked.
howToServe: Always cooked — scrambled or hard-boiled — with no added salt or fat, in a very small amount.
avoid: Raw egg: risk of salmonella, and the avidin in raw egg white blocks biotin absorption.
tip: A small piece of cooked egg once a week is plenty.

name: Fruits & vegetables
description: Some fruits and vegetables, such as courgette, cooked carrot, watermelon or melon, can be given in small amounts.
whyGood: They add fibre and hydration alongside the main diet.
howToServe: Cooked or raw depending on the vegetable, cut into small pieces, in very small amounts.
avoid: Onion, garlic, leek, grapes and avocado, which are toxic to cats.
tip: Fruits and vegetables never replace a cat's need for animal protein.

name: Dairy
description: Most adult cats are lactose intolerant, so dairy should stay very occasional.
whyGood: A little hard cheese or plain yoghurt is tolerated by some cats.
howToServe: In very small amounts, occasionally, and never cow's milk.
avoid: Cow's milk often causes diarrhoea and digestive upset in adult cats.
tip: If your cat likes milk, choose a lactose-free milk made for cats.

name: Dangerous foods
description: Chocolate, onion, garlic, grapes, avocado and xylitol are among the most toxic foods for cats.
avoid: Can cause vomiting, diarrhoea, agitation, tremors, damage to red blood cells or seizures, and can be fatal depending on the amount eaten.
tip: Never give these foods to your cat, in any form. If your cat has eaten one, contact your vet or an emergency veterinary service immediately.
